units.title: Time and Space
units.overview: Welcome to Year 6! We begin with a journey through time and space. You will read two science fiction stories: one about a boy who meets his older self, and one about a girl sailing a solar yacht home from the Moon all on her own. You will learn how science fiction stories are built, how to use clauses and punctuation like a confident writer, and then you will invent a science fiction story of your own.
objectives: Explain the structure of a science fiction story (exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution) and its typical features.
Recognise simple, compound and complex sentences, and main and subordinate clauses.
Use parenthesis with brackets, commas and dashes to add extra information.
Use colons, semi-colons and ellipses correctly and for effect.
Spell words with the different spellings of the /k/ sound.
Listen to a science fiction story and answer questions about it.
Plan, draft and improve your own science fiction story.

texts.title: Time Travel
texts.kind: Science fiction story by Jenny Hogan
texts.summary: The narrator is a careful boy who lives by three rules, and one of them is never to have anything to do with time travel. Then he is pulled forward in time into his own bedroom, where he meets his older self. His older self needs him to win the school science fair, because winning leads to a science scholarship, and that is how time travel will one day be invented. After an accident, the narrator has to rebuild his volcano project, and an unexpected trip far back into the past adds to the adventure.

texts.title: Solo Solar Sailing
texts.kind: Science fiction story by Zareh MacPherson
texts.summary: A young girl is sailing her solar yacht, the Helios, home from the Moon on her own, the youngest girl ever to try. Written as a series of log entries, the story follows her as alarms warn of a huge solar flare. She must adjust the solar sail and the ion tiller to stay on course for Earth, remembering her father’s advice that solar sailing is more an art than a science.

texts.title: Galileo!
texts.summary: Stella seems to be at school, but her school is in virtual reality. When she switches it off, we discover that she is really aboard her mother’s spaceship, exploring the galaxy, and that a wormhole is causing trouble.

grammar.title: Simple, compound and complex sentences
grammar.intro: Good writers mix their sentences like a chef mixes flavours. Short ones create drama; longer ones explain and describe. In Year 6, you will choose your sentence type on purpose, so let’s make sure you know all three.
points: A **simple sentence** has one main clause: ‘The time machine hummed.’
A **compound sentence** joins two main clauses with a coordinating conjunction such as **and**, **but**, **or** or **so**.
A **complex sentence** has a main clause and at least one **subordinate clause**, often starting with **because**, **when**, **if**, **although** or **while**.
Each main clause in a compound sentence makes sense on its own. A subordinate clause does not.

examples.text: The volcano exploded.
examples.note: Simple: one main clause.

examples.text: The volcano exploded, so I had to build another one.
examples.note: Compound: two main clauses joined by ‘so’.

examples.text: Because the volcano exploded, I had to build another one.
examples.note: Complex: the subordinate clause starts with ‘because’.

grammar.tip: Ask yourself: can each part stand on its own as a sentence? If both can, it is compound. If one cannot, it is complex.

practice.q: Which sentence is simple?
options: The rocket launched and the crowd cheered.
When the rocket launched, the crowd cheered.
The rocket launched, but the crowd was silent.
practice.explain: ‘The rocket launched at dawn.’ has only one main clause.

practice.q: Which sentence is compound?
options: Although it was late, we watched the stars.
We watched the stars, but the clouds soon covered them.
Because it was clear, we watched the stars.
practice.explain: Two main clauses are joined by ‘but’, so the sentence is compound.

practice.q: Which sentence is complex?
options: I opened the door and walked in.
I opened the door when I heard a strange humming.
I opened the door, so the cat ran out.
practice.explain: ‘when I heard a strange humming’ is a subordinate clause, so the sentence is complex.

practice.q: Which word would turn ‘The alarm rang. We woke up.’ into a complex sentence?
practice.explain: ‘When the alarm rang, we woke up.’ ‘When’ starts a subordinate clause.

practice.q: What type of sentence is this? ‘You can travel to the past, or you can visit the future.’
practice.explain: Two main clauses are joined by ‘or’, so it is compound.

grammar.title: Parenthesis
grammar.intro: Sometimes you want to whisper a little extra detail to your reader in the middle of a sentence. That is what parenthesis does! It adds information without breaking the sentence.
points: **Parenthesis** is a word, phrase or clause added to a sentence to give extra information.
You can mark it with a pair of **brackets** ( ), a pair of **commas** or a pair of **dashes** (–).
Dashes make the extra information stand out more; brackets make it quieter.
If you take the parenthesis away, the sentence must still make sense.

examples.text: My older self (who looked very confident) handed me a note.
examples.note: Brackets around the extra information.

examples.text: The science fair, I was sure, would be a disaster.
examples.note: A pair of commas.

examples.text: The volcano – my second attempt – finally worked.
examples.note: A pair of dashes makes the detail stand out.

grammar.tip: Parenthesis always comes in pairs, unless it reaches the end of the sentence. Check that you have opened and closed it.

practice.q: Which sentence uses brackets for parenthesis correctly?
options: The comet (a ball of ice and dust) flew past.
The comet a ball (of ice and dust flew) past.
(The comet a ball) of ice and dust flew past.
The comet a ball of ice and dust (flew past).
practice.explain: The brackets surround the extra information, ‘a ball of ice and dust’.

practice.q: Which words are the parenthesis? ‘Mrs Patel, our science teacher, judged the fair.’
practice.explain: ‘our science teacher’ is extra information, marked by a pair of commas.

practice.q: Which sentence uses dashes correctly?
options: The yacht – built in 2070 sailed home.
The yacht – built in 2070 – sailed home.
The yacht built – in 2070 – sailed home.
– The yacht built in 2070 sailed home.
practice.explain: A pair of dashes goes around the extra information.

practice.q: What happens when you remove the parenthesis from a sentence?
practice.explain: Parenthesis is extra information, so the sentence still makes sense without it.

practice.q: Which punctuation can NOT be used to mark parenthesis?
practice.explain: Parenthesis is marked with brackets, commas or dashes.

grammar.title: Main and subordinate clauses
grammar.intro: Think of the main clause as the captain of the sentence and the subordinate clause as the crew. The crew adds useful information, but it cannot sail the ship alone!
points: A **main clause** has a subject and a verb and makes sense on its own.
A **subordinate clause** also has a verb, but it depends on the main clause to make sense.
Subordinate clauses often begin with **subordinating conjunctions** (if, until, because, although, unless, since) or **relative pronouns** (who, which, that).
When a subordinate clause comes first, put a comma after it.

examples.text: **I will reach Earth** __if the sail holds__.
examples.note: The main clause is in bold; the subordinate clause is underlined.

examples.text: __Unless I change direction__, **I will drift towards Mars**.
examples.note: The subordinate clause comes first, so it is followed by a comma.

examples.text: **She checked the instruments**, __which were flashing red__.
examples.note: A relative pronoun begins this subordinate clause.

grammar.tip: Read each clause aloud on its own. The one that sounds unfinished is the subordinate clause.

practice.q: Which is the main clause? ‘Although the flare was huge, the narrator stayed calm.’
practice.explain: ‘the narrator stayed calm’ makes sense on its own.

practice.q: Which is the subordinate clause? ‘We will wait here until the storm passes.’
practice.explain: ‘until the storm passes’ cannot stand on its own.

practice.q: Which word often begins a subordinate clause?
practice.explain: ‘Unless’ is a subordinating conjunction.

practice.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: If the alarm rings we must act fast.
If the alarm rings, we must act fast.
If, the alarm rings we must act fast.
If the alarm, rings we must act fast.
practice.explain: The subordinate clause comes first, so a comma follows it.

practice.q: Which of these is a main clause?
practice.explain: ‘the astronaut smiled’ has a subject and a verb and makes sense alone.

grammar.title: Colons, semi-colons and ellipses
grammar.intro: These three marks are a Year 6 writer’s secret tools. Use them well, and your writing will look polished and sound exciting. Let’s learn what each one does.
points: A **colon** (:) introduces something: a list, an explanation or a quotation. The words before it must make a complete sentence.
A **semi-colon** (;) joins two main clauses that are closely linked. Both parts must make sense on their own.
An **ellipsis** (…) shows a pause, builds suspense, or shows that words have been left out.

examples.text: I packed three things: a torch, a map and a compass.
examples.note: The colon introduces a list.

examples.text: The alarm stopped; the danger had passed.
examples.note: The semi-colon joins two linked main clauses.

examples.text: The door creaked open … and then there was silence.
examples.note: The ellipsis builds suspense.

grammar.tip: Test a semi-colon by replacing it with a full stop. If you get two proper sentences, the semi-colon is correct.

practice.q: Which sentence uses a colon correctly?
options: We need three things: food, water and fuel.
We: need three things food, water and fuel.
We need three: things food, water and fuel.
practice.explain: The colon comes after a complete sentence and introduces the list.

practice.q: Which sentence uses a semi-colon correctly?
options: The sun rose; the sky turned gold.
The sun; rose the sky turned gold.
The sun rose the; sky turned gold.
The; sun rose the sky turned gold.
practice.explain: The semi-colon joins two linked main clauses.

practice.q: What is an ellipsis often used for in a story?
practice.explain: An ellipsis makes the reader pause and wonder what will happen next.

practice.q: Which mark introduces an explanation? ‘There was only one problem _ the engine had stopped.’
practice.explain: A colon introduces the explanation: ‘the engine had stopped’.

practice.q: Which of these is an ellipsis?
practice.explain: An ellipsis is three dots.

units.title: Saving Our Oceans
units.overview: Our oceans cover most of our planet, and the creatures in them need our help. In this unit you will read two arguments about marine life: one that argues strongly for protecting whales, and one that weighs up whether ships are the biggest threat to sea creatures. You will learn how writers build an argument, how to use formal language and the passive voice, and then you will write a powerful argument of your own.
objectives: Identify the features of one-sided and balanced arguments.
Use active and passive verbs, and explain why writers choose the passive voice in formal writing.
Use linking adverbials and opening phrases to connect ideas in an argument.
Add prefixes and suffixes to root words, and work out what new words mean.
Choose the correct quantifiers for countable and uncountable nouns.
Listen to a balanced argument and identify the facts and the writer’s final point of view.
Plan and write a one-sided argument and an argumentative essay.

texts.title: Whales are Good for Our Planet!
texts.summary: This argument tells us that whales are our friends in the fight against climate change. Over its long life, a whale stores a huge amount of carbon in its body, far more than a tree. Whales also help tiny phytoplankton to grow, and phytoplankton take in carbon dioxide too. The writer adds that whale watching helps coastal communities to earn a living, and concludes that we must protect whales.

texts.title: Are Ships the Main Threat to Marine Life?
texts.summary: This argument looks at both sides. Ships can strike marine animals, their noise confuses creatures that use echolocation, and oil spills and overfishing cause great harm. However, ships are important for trade and food. The writer concludes that ships are only one of the threats to marine life, and that ships can be made kinder to the ocean, for example by travelling more slowly.

texts.title: Is Climate Change the Main Cause of the Decline in Whale Populations?
texts.summary: A balanced argument about whether climate change is the main reason why whale numbers have fallen. It explains how warming oceans affect the whales’ food, and it considers other human activities that may also play a part.

vocab.meaning: A piece of writing that gives reasons to persuade the reader to agree with a point of view.
vocab.example: Her argument was full of facts and strong reasons.

vocab.meaning: An argument that gives the reasons for only one point of view.
vocab.example: The article about whales is a one-sided argument.

vocab.meaning: An argument that gives both sides before the writer gives a final opinion.
vocab.example: A balanced argument helps readers to make up their own minds.

vocab.meaning: A gas released when fuels are burnt. Too much of it in the air warms our planet.
vocab.example: Trees and phytoplankton take in carbon dioxide.

vocab.meaning: Tiny, plant-like living things that float near the surface of the sea.
vocab.example: Phytoplankton are so small that you need a microscope to see them.

vocab.meaning: Long-term changes in the Earth’s temperature and weather patterns.
vocab.example: Climate change is making some oceans warmer.

vocab.meaning: Sea creatures that are caught in fishing nets by accident.
vocab.example: Dolphins and turtles are sometimes caught as bycatch.

vocab.meaning: A way some animals find their way by sending out sounds and listening to the echoes.
vocab.example: Loud ships can confuse whales that use echolocation.

vocab.meaning: A way of writing in which the thing that receives the action becomes the subject of the sentence.
vocab.example: ‘Carbon is stored by whales’ is written in the passive voice.

vocab.meaning: A word that tells us how much or how many, such as many, much, few, less or some.
vocab.example: There are fewer whales than there once were.

grammar.title: Active and passive verbs
grammar.intro: Have you noticed how formal writing sometimes sounds a bit like a science report? That is often because of the passive voice. Learning to switch between active and passive gives you real control over your writing.
points: In the **active voice**, the subject does the action: ‘Whales **store** carbon.’
In the **passive voice**, the subject has the action done to it: ‘Carbon **is stored** by whales.’
The passive is made with a form of **be** (is, are, was, were, will be) plus the **past participle** (stored, written, caught).
Writers use the passive in formal writing, or when the doer is unknown or not important.

examples.text: Scientists **studied** the whales.
examples.note: Active: the scientists did the studying.

examples.text: The whales **were studied** by scientists.
examples.note: Passive: the whales had the action done to them.

examples.text: The nets **were removed** from the reef.
examples.note: Passive without ‘by’: we do not need to know who did it.

grammar.tip: If you can add ‘by …’ after the verb and it makes sense, the sentence is probably passive.

practice.q: Which sentence is active?

practice.explain: The subject, ‘the diver’, does the action.

practice.q: Which sentence is passive?

practice.explain: ‘was cleaned’ is a form of ‘be’ plus a past participle, so it is passive.

practice.q: Change to the passive: ‘The children planted the trees.’
options: The trees were planted by the children.
practice.explain: The object, ‘the trees’, becomes the subject, and we use ‘were planted’.

practice.q: Change to the active: ‘The article was written by Maya.’
practice.explain: Maya did the writing, so she becomes the subject.

practice.q: Why might a writer choose the passive voice?
options: To focus on the action when the doer is not important
practice.explain: The passive puts the focus on the action or the thing affected.

grammar.title: Linking adverbials
grammar.intro: An argument is like a bridge made of ideas. Linking adverbials are the bolts that hold it together, guiding your reader smoothly from one point to the next.
points: **Linking adverbials** connect ideas across sentences and paragraphs.
To **add** a point: furthermore, moreover, in addition, besides.
To **compare**: similarly, likewise. To **contrast**: however, on the other hand.
To show a **result**: consequently, therefore, as a result.
When a linking adverbial starts a sentence, put a comma after it.

examples.text: Whales store carbon. **Furthermore**, they help phytoplankton to grow.
examples.note: Adds a second point.

examples.text: Plastic harms turtles. **Similarly**, it harms seabirds.
examples.note: Shows that two ideas are alike.

examples.text: Ships carry our food. **However**, they can harm sea creatures.
examples.note: Shows the other side.

grammar.tip: Do not use ‘and’ or ‘but’ to start every sentence. Swap in a linking adverbial instead.

practice.q: Which linking adverbial shows a contrast?
practice.explain: ‘However’ introduces a different or opposite idea.

practice.q: Which linking adverbial shows that two things are alike?
practice.explain: ‘Similarly’ compares two ideas.

practice.q: Choose the best word: ‘Whales attract tourists. ___, tourism creates jobs.’
practice.explain: We are adding a further point, so ‘In addition’ fits.

practice.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
practice.explain: Put a comma after a linking adverbial at the start of a sentence.

practice.q: Which linking adverbial shows a result?
practice.explain: ‘Consequently’ means ‘as a result’.

grammar.title: Quantifiers
grammar.intro: How many fish are in the sea? How much plastic is in the ocean? Quantifiers help you to answer questions like these precisely, and choosing the right one is a sign of a careful writer.
points: A **quantifier** tells us how much or how many.
**Countable nouns** can be counted (whales, nets): use **many**, **few**, **fewer**.
**Uncountable nouns** cannot be counted (water, pollution): use **much**, **little**, **less**.
**Some**, **any**, **a lot of** and **plenty of** work with both.
We usually use **any** in questions and negative sentences: ‘Are there any sharks?’

examples.text: There are **fewer** whales than there were a hundred years ago.
examples.note: Whales can be counted.

examples.text: We should use **less** plastic.
examples.note: Plastic (as a material) is uncountable.

examples.text: How **much** oil was spilt? How **many** birds were affected?
examples.note: ‘much’ for uncountable, ‘many’ for countable.

grammar.tip: Try putting a number in front of the noun. If ‘three whales’ works, use many or fewer.

practice.q: Choose the correct word: ‘There is ___ rubbish on the beach today.’
practice.explain: Rubbish is uncountable, so we use ‘less’.

practice.q: Choose the correct word: ‘How ___ dolphins did you see?’
practice.explain: Dolphins can be counted, so we use ‘many’.

practice.q: Which noun is uncountable?
practice.explain: We cannot count water, so it is uncountable.

practice.q: Choose the correct sentence.
options: There are less fish this year.
There are fewer fish this year.
There are much fish this year.
There is many fish this year.
practice.explain: Fish can be counted here, so ‘fewer’ is correct.

practice.q: Which quantifier fits a question? ‘Are there ___ turtles in this bay?’
practice.explain: We usually use ‘any’ in questions.

units.title: Stories From The Sea
units.overview: Hoist the sails! This unit is full of salty sea air and daring adventures. You will read about a clever boy who outwits egg pirates, and about a girl whose best friend is a one-legged seagull. Both stories use flashbacks, so you will learn how a memory from the past can change what happens next. Then you will write your own adventure story with a flashback.
objectives: Explain what a flashback is and how it affects the plot of an adventure story.
Use adverbs and adverbial phrases of time, place and manner.
Recognise similes, metaphors, personification, onomatopoeia, alliteration and idioms.
Use suffixes to change the word class of a word.
Use relative pronouns and relative clauses to add information.
Punctuate direct speech correctly and change it into reported speech.
Speak confidently and fluently, and write an adventure story with a flashback.

texts.title: Yao Bai and the Egg Pirates
texts.summary: Long ago, at the time of the California gold rush, Yao Bai sails out with his father and uncle to collect seabird eggs from the islands near San Francisco to sell in the city. The family is poor and needs the money, but the sea is home to egg pirates. When the pirates come, Yao remembers something from a fishing trip the week before, and his clever idea saves the family’s eggs.

texts.title: Katie and Gulliver
texts.summary: Every holiday, Katie stays with her uncle near the harbour, where a big one-legged seagull called Gulliver seems to watch over her. Flashbacks show how Gulliver has raised the alarm whenever Katie was in danger. When Katie ends up stranded on a rock, and Gulliver has gone missing, the story asks whether her loyal friend could still be looking after her.

grammar.title: Adverbs and adverbial phrases
grammar.intro: Adverbs are the storyteller’s secret ingredient. They tell your reader exactly how, when and where things happen, so a plain sentence becomes a vivid scene.
points: An **adverb** gives more information about a verb. Many adverbs end in **-ly**: grimly, quickly, fearfully.
An **adverbial phrase** is a group of words that does the same job: ‘at last’, ‘over the side’, ‘early that morning’.
Adverbs and adverbials can tell us about **manner** (how), **time** (when) and **place** (where).
You can move an adverbial to the front of a sentence for effect. Put a comma after it: ‘At dawn, they set sail.’

examples.text: Yao whispered **fearfully**.
examples.note: Manner: how he whispered.

examples.text: **Early that morning**, they rowed to the island.
examples.note: Time: when they rowed. The fronted adverbial is followed by a comma.

examples.text: They lowered the nets **over the side of the boat**.
examples.note: Place: where they lowered the nets.

grammar.tip: Ask the verb a question: how? when? where? The answer is your adverb or adverbial.

practice.q: Which word is an adverb? ‘The pirates rowed silently towards the boat.’
practice.explain: ‘silently’ tells us how they rowed.

practice.q: What does the adverbial phrase tell us? ‘They sailed home at sunset.’
practice.explain: ‘at sunset’ tells us when.

practice.q: Which is an adverbial phrase of place?
practice.explain: ‘under the nets’ tells us where.

practice.q: Which sentence uses a fronted adverbial correctly?
options: In the morning the boat left.
In the morning, the boat left.
In, the morning the boat left.
In the morning the, boat left.
practice.explain: Put a comma after a fronted adverbial.

practice.q: Which adverb tells us how?
practice.explain: ‘carefully’ describes the manner of an action.

grammar.title: Relative pronouns and clauses
grammar.intro: Relative clauses let you slip extra detail about a person or thing into your sentence without starting a new one. They make your writing flow like the tide.
points: A **relative clause** gives more information about a noun. It starts with a **relative pronoun**.
Use **who** for people, **which** for things and animals, **that** for people or things, **whose** for belonging and **whom** for people when they are the object.
If the information is extra and not essential, put **commas** around the relative clause.
If the information is essential to know which one we mean, do not use commas: ‘The boat **that we borrowed** was blue.’

examples.text: Katie, **who loved the harbour**, visited every holiday.
examples.note: Extra information about Katie, so commas are used.

examples.text: The gull **that only had one leg** was Gulliver.
examples.note: Essential information that tells us which gull, so no commas.

examples.text: The sailor **whose boat was damaged** asked for help.
examples.note: ‘whose’ shows that the boat belonged to the sailor.

grammar.tip: Take out a relative clause in commas. If the sentence still makes sense, the commas are right.

practice.q: Choose the correct pronoun: ‘Uncle Ralph, ___ lived near the harbour, carved a bird.’
practice.explain: Uncle Ralph is a person and the subject of ‘lived’, so we use ‘who’.

practice.q: Choose the correct pronoun: ‘The net, ___ was full of shrimp, was heavy.’
practice.explain: A net is a thing, so we use ‘which’.

practice.q: Which is the relative clause? ‘The boy whose idea saved the eggs was Yao.’
practice.explain: The relative clause begins with ‘whose’ and tells us more about the boy.

practice.q: Which pronoun shows belonging?
practice.explain: ‘whose’ shows that something belongs to someone.

practice.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: Gulliver which was a seagull, had one leg.
Gulliver, which was a seagull, had one leg.
Gulliver, which was a seagull had one leg.
Gulliver which, was a seagull had one leg.
practice.explain: The extra information needs a comma on each side.

grammar.title: Direct speech
grammar.intro: Dialogue brings characters to life. When your reader can ‘hear’ them speak, your story feels real. Let’s make sure every word they say is punctuated perfectly.
points: **Direct speech** shows the exact words a character says, inside **inverted commas** (“ ”).
Punctuation that belongs to the spoken words goes **inside** the inverted commas: “Look!” cried Katie.
If the speech comes first, end it with a comma, question mark or exclamation mark, not a full stop, before ‘said’.
Start a **new line** each time a different person speaks.
**Reported speech** tells us what someone said without inverted commas: Katie said that she was cold.

examples.text: “The tide is coming in,” said Dad.
examples.note: The comma goes inside the inverted commas.

examples.text: Uncle Ralph asked, “Have you seen Gulliver?”
examples.note: A comma after ‘asked’, and the question mark inside.

examples.text: Katie said that she had heard a seagull.
examples.note: Reported speech: no inverted commas.

grammar.tip: Read your dialogue aloud. If it sounds like natural talking, you have probably got it right.

practice.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
practice.explain: The comma goes inside the closing inverted commas.

practice.q: Which is reported speech?
options: Katie said that she was cold.
practice.explain: Reported speech has no inverted commas and usually uses ‘that’.

practice.q: When should you start a new line in dialogue?
options: Only at the end of a chapter
practice.explain: Each new speaker starts on a new line.

practice.q: Which is correct?
practice.explain: A comma after ‘asked’, and the question mark inside the inverted commas.

practice.q: What are inverted commas used for?
options: To show the exact words someone says
practice.explain: Inverted commas go around the exact words spoken.

units.title: Innovators and Inventors
units.overview: What does it take to change the world? In this unit you will meet remarkable people who did just that: a writer at the Japanese imperial court more than a thousand years ago, a brilliant mathematician who helped astronauts reach the Moon, and an American inventor who was also a printer, a writer and a statesman. You will learn how biographies are organised, how to use sentences for different effects, and then you will write a biography of your own.
objectives: Explain the structure and features of a biography, including chronological order and the third person.
Use short, long, compound and complex sentences for different effects.
Use context clues to work out the meanings of unfamiliar words.
Tell the difference between homographs and homophones.
Use subordinate clauses and connectives for emphasis, such as ‘not only … but also’.
Use adverbs and adverbial phrases of time to show when events happened.
Listen to a talk about an inventor, then plan and write a biography.

texts.title: Murasaki Shikibu – Life at the Imperial Court
texts.summary: Murasaki Shikibu was born in Japan in about 978. As a child, she learnt to write Chinese, which only men were usually taught at the time. She served at the imperial court, and her experiences there helped her to write The Tale of Genji, which is often called the world’s first novel.

texts.title: Katherine Johnson – Racing to the Moon
texts.summary: Katherine Johnson was born in 1918 and showed a gift for numbers from an early age. She grew up in a segregated society with few schools for black children, but she became a brilliant mathematician. Her calculations helped to plot the flight paths of American spacecraft, including missions to the Moon.

texts.title: Benjamin Franklin – Statesman, Businessman and Inventor
texts.summary: Benjamin Franklin was born in Boston in 1706 into a large family. He worked in his father’s candle and soap business and then in his brother’s print shop, reading every book he could. He learnt that nothing dishonest is truly useful. He invented the lightning rod, swim fins, a library chair and an extension arm, and he helped to draft the Declaration of Independence. He believed inventions should be shared freely.

texts.title: Elon Musk’s Amazing Inventions

grammar.title: Using sentences for different effects
grammar.intro: Writing is a bit like music. If every note is the same length, it becomes dull. When you mix short and long sentences, your writing has rhythm, and your reader stays with you all the way.
points: **Short sentences** create impact, drama or tension: ‘She did it.’
**Long sentences** (compound or complex) add detail and explain ideas.
Joining short sentences with **conjunctions** or **relative clauses** helps writing to flow.
Varying sentence length changes the **pace** and keeps the reader interested.

examples.text: The calculations were checked again and again, because one tiny mistake could put the astronauts in danger. They were perfect.
examples.note: A long sentence explains; the short one adds impact.

examples.text: The numbers were checked. Then they were checked again. Nothing could go wrong.
examples.note: Short sentences build tension and emphasis.

examples.text: Franklin, who loved books, built a chair that turned into steps.
examples.note: A relative clause joins two ideas smoothly.

grammar.tip: Read your work aloud. If it sounds choppy, join some sentences. If it sounds breathless, split some up.

practice.q: What effect does a very short sentence usually have?

practice.explain: Short sentences stand out and create drama.

Because Ben loved books, he built a library chair.

practice.explain: A subordinate clause with ‘because’ joins the ideas correctly.

practice.q: Why do writers vary sentence length?
options: To change the pace and keep readers interested
To make writing harder to read
practice.explain: Varied sentences give writing rhythm and pace.

practice.q: Which sentence is a long complex sentence?
options: When the numbers were finally checked, the team knew the mission was safe.
practice.explain: It has a subordinate clause and a main clause, so it is complex.

practice.q: Which would make the most dramatic ending to a paragraph?

They went home later that evening after the meeting.
It was quite a long day for everyone.
practice.explain: A one-word sentence can create a powerful, dramatic ending.

grammar.title: Subordinate clauses and connectives for emphasis
grammar.intro: Want your reader to notice something important? Subordinate clauses add detail, and special connectives put a spotlight on your ideas. Let’s add some power to your sentences!
points: A **subordinate clause** adds information to a main clause and cannot stand alone.
Subordinate clauses can begin with words such as **although**, **while**, **when**, **before** and **because**.
**Connectives for emphasis** make a point stronger: **not only … but also**, **neither … nor**, **no sooner … than**, **especially**, **particularly**.
When a sentence starts with ‘Not only’, the order of the words changes: ‘Not only **did he** read, but he also wrote.’

examples.text: Although he left school at the age of ten, Ben never stopped learning.
examples.note: The subordinate clause comes first, followed by a comma.

examples.text: Ben was **not only** a printer **but also** an inventor.
examples.note: The connective emphasises both roles.

examples.text: **No sooner** had he finished one book **than** he started another.
examples.note: This shows that something happened straight after something else.

grammar.tip: Use connectives for emphasis carefully. One or two in a paragraph is plenty.

practice.q: Which is the subordinate clause? ‘While he worked in the shop, Ben read every night.’
options: While he worked in the shop
practice.explain: ‘While he worked in the shop’ cannot stand alone.

practice.q: Complete the connective: ‘Neither Ben ___ his friends thought it was wrong.’
practice.explain: ‘Neither’ is paired with ‘nor’.

practice.q: Complete: ‘Not only did she solve the problem, ___ she also explained it.’
practice.explain: ‘Not only’ is paired with ‘but also’.

practice.q: Which sentence is correct?
options: No sooner had the storm started than the lights went out.
No sooner the storm started than the lights went out.
No sooner had the storm started when the lights went out.
No sooner had the storm started but the lights went out.
practice.explain: We say ‘No sooner had … than …’.

practice.q: Which word adds emphasis? ‘Ben loved swimming, ___ in the river.’
practice.explain: ‘especially’ emphasises where he loved swimming most.

grammar.title: Adverbs and adverbial phrases of time
grammar.intro: A biography is a journey through someone’s life. Adverbials of time are the signposts that show your reader where they are on that journey.
points: **Adverbs of time** tell us when: later, soon, then, finally, afterwards.
**Adverbial phrases of time** do the same job with more words: ‘as a boy’, ‘in 1790’, ‘two centuries later’, ‘when he was 17’.
They are often used at the start of a sentence (a **fronted adverbial**), followed by a comma.
They help to keep events in **chronological order**.

examples.text: **As a boy,** Franklin loved to swim.
examples.note: A fronted adverbial phrase of time, followed by a comma.

examples.text: **Later,** he moved to Philadelphia.
examples.note: A single adverb of time.

examples.text: She retired from NASA **in 1986**.
examples.note: The adverbial can also come at the end.

grammar.tip: Do not start every sentence the same way. Vary your adverbials: ‘Soon’, ‘Years later’, ‘By then’.

practice.q: Which is an adverbial phrase of time?
practice.explain: ‘two years later’ tells us when.

practice.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
practice.explain: Put a comma after a fronted adverbial.

practice.q: Which word is an adverb of time?
practice.explain: ‘afterwards’ tells us when.

practice.q: Why are adverbials of time useful in a biography?

practice.explain: They help to keep events in chronological order.

practice.q: Find the adverbial of time: ‘When she was ten, Katherine started high school.’

units.title: Nature
units.overview: Step outside and listen! In this unit you will read poems inspired by the natural world: an eagle on a cliff, a spider spinning its web, a field of golden daffodils, a stormy night and a quiet snowy wood. You will explore the themes and images in poems, choose words with exactly the right shade of meaning, and learn how rhyme schemes work. Then you will write an acrostic poem and a poem with rhyming couplets.
objectives: Identify the themes of poems and explain how poets show them.
Choose words with the right shade of meaning to create atmosphere.
Explain how imagery, such as similes, metaphors and personification, creates pictures in the reader’s mind.
Spell words with the consonant blends ch and tch.
Identify rhyme schemes and rhyming couplets.
Use synonyms and antonyms to make writing precise and interesting.
Perform a poem aloud, and write an acrostic poem and a poem with rhyming couplets.

grammar.title: Shades of meaning
grammar.intro: Poets are word detectives. They hunt for the one word that fits exactly. Is a light flickering, glowing or blazing? Each choice paints a different picture, and now you can choose like a poet too.
points: Words with **similar meanings** can still have **different strengths** or feelings.
Put similar words on a **scale**: flickering → glowing → blazing; still → hushed → tranquil.
This works for **adjectives**, **verbs** and **adverbs**: walk → stride → march; quietly → silently.
Choose the shade that fits your **mood** and **theme**.

examples.text: The candle **flickered** in the draught.
examples.note: A weak, unsteady light.

examples.text: The fire **blazed** across the hillside.
examples.note: A strong, fierce light.

examples.text: The wind **whispered** … the wind **howled**.
examples.note: The verbs create two very different moods.

grammar.tip: Ask: is this word too strong, too weak or just right for the mood?

grammar.title: Imagery in poetry
grammar.intro: Close your eyes and listen to a good poem. Can you see it? That is imagery at work. These tools help your reader see, hear and feel your words.
points: A **simile** compares two things using **like** or **as**: ‘as quick as a lightning bolt’.
A **metaphor** says one thing **is** another: ‘The clouds were cotton balls.’
**Personification** gives human qualities to things that are not human: ‘The wind ran away with the papers.’
**Alliteration** repeats the first sound of nearby words; **onomatopoeia** uses words that sound like their meaning.

examples.text: The eagle fell **like a thunderbolt**.
examples.note: A simile.

examples.text: The leaves **drank** the rain.
examples.note: Personification: leaves cannot really drink.

examples.text: **S**ilver **s**treams **s**parkled.
examples.note: Alliteration with the /s/ sound.

grammar.tip: When you spot an image, explain what it makes you picture AND how it makes you feel.

practice.explain: The /b/ sound is repeated.

grammar.title: Synonyms and antonyms
grammar.intro: Using the same word again and again is like eating the same lunch every day. Synonyms give your writing variety, and antonyms help you to show contrast.
points: A **synonym** has the same or nearly the same meaning: huge, enormous, gigantic.
An **antonym** has the opposite meaning: calm and stormy; trust and doubt.
Some antonyms are made with **prefixes**: happy and unhappy; possible and impossible.
A **thesaurus** helps you to find synonyms and antonyms.

examples.text: The pool was noisy, but under the water it was **silent**.
examples.note: ‘Noisy’ and ‘silent’ are antonyms that show contrast.

examples.text: She was **exhausted** after the swim.
examples.note: A stronger synonym for ‘tired’.

examples.text: The leaves **tumbled** and **toppled** from the trees.
examples.note: Two synonyms that also create alliteration.

grammar.tip: After using a thesaurus, always check that the new word fits the sentence.

units.title: Looking After Our Planet
units.overview: How should we power our homes, schools and cities without harming the Earth? In this unit you will read persuasive articles about wind, sun, water and other sources of energy. Some writers love wind farms, and some do not! You will learn the tricks persuasive writers use, practise indirect speech, word classes and verb forms, and then write a persuasive news article of your own.
objectives: Identify persuasive devices, such as rhetorical questions, short emphatic statements and emotive language.
Tell the difference between facts and opinions, and between persuasive and argumentative texts.
Change direct speech into indirect (reported) speech, including questions.
Spell words with the suffixes -tion, -cian, -sion, -ssion, -ence and -ance.
Identify word classes, including determiners, prepositions and conjunctions.
Use different verb forms, including participles.
Give a short presentation, and write a persuasive paragraph and a persuasive news article.

texts.title: The Wind: A Clean and Abundant Energy Source
texts.summary: This article persuades us that wind is a wonderful source of energy. People have used the wind for a very long time to sail boats, pump water and grind grain. Today, wind turbines turn it into electricity without polluting the air, and because the wind will never run out, it is renewable.

texts.title: Please – No More Wind Farms!
texts.summary: This writer takes the opposite view. Wind turbines can harm birds and bats, spoil the landscape, and only work when the wind blows, so they are not always reliable. The writer uses strong, emotive words to persuade us that no more wind farms should be built.

texts.title: Renewable Sources of Energy – The Way Forward
texts.summary: This article looks at several renewable sources of energy, including geothermal, biomass, hydroelectric and solar power, and weighs up their advantages and disadvantages. The writer’s aim is to persuade us that solar energy is the best choice, because it is clean, increasingly affordable, portable and available to people almost everywhere.

vocab.example: Wind and sunlight are renewable sources of energy.

vocab.meaning: Fuels such as coal, oil and gas, formed underground over millions of years. They will run out.
vocab.example: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide.

vocab.meaning: A tall machine with large blades that turns the energy of the wind into electricity.
vocab.example: The wind turbine’s blades turned slowly in the breeze.

vocab.meaning: Trying to make someone agree with an opinion or do something.
vocab.example: Her persuasive speech made everyone want to recycle.

vocab.meaning: A question asked for effect, not because the writer expects an answer.
vocab.example: ‘Who wouldn’t want clean air?’ is a rhetorical question.

vocab.meaning: Words chosen to make the reader feel strong emotions.
vocab.example: Calling turbines ‘monstrosities’ is emotive language.

vocab.meaning: Heat from deep inside the Earth.
vocab.example: Iceland uses geothermal energy to heat many homes.

vocab.meaning: Electricity made from the power of moving water.
vocab.example: The dam powers a hydroelectric power station.

vocab.meaning: Reporting what someone said or asked without using their exact words.
vocab.example: She asked whether the wind farm was finished.

vocab.meaning: A word that comes before a noun to show which one or how many, such as the, a, some or this.
vocab.example: In ‘some panels’, ‘some’ is a determiner.

grammar.title: More about indirect speech
grammar.intro: Reporters, scientists and storytellers all need to tell us what other people said. Indirect speech lets you do that smoothly. Today we will focus on reporting questions, which is a real Year 6 skill.
points: **Indirect (reported) speech** tells us what someone said without using their exact words or inverted commas.
The tense usually moves **back**: is → was; can → could; will → would.
**Pronouns** and time words change: ‘I’ → he or she; ‘today’ → that day.
To report a yes/no question, use **if** or **whether**: She asked **if** I had seen it.
To report a wh- question, keep the question word but use **statement word order**, and end with a full stop: He asked where the turbines **were**.

examples.text: “Is wind power free?” asked Leo. → Leo asked if wind power was free.
examples.note: A yes/no question reported with ‘if’.

examples.text: “Why do we burn coal?” the writer asked. → The writer asked why we burned coal.
examples.note: The question word stays, but the word order changes.

examples.text: “I will plant trees,” said Mina. → Mina said that she would plant trees.
examples.note: The tense and the pronoun change.

grammar.tip: No question marks in indirect questions! They are statements about a question.

practice.q: Report this: “Can we use solar panels?” asked Sam.
options: Sam asked if they could use solar panels.
Sam asked can we use solar panels?
Sam asked, “if they could use solar panels.”
Sam asked could they use solar panels.
practice.explain: Use ‘if’, change ‘can’ to ‘could’ and ‘we’ to ‘they’, and end with a full stop.

practice.q: Which indirect question is correct?
options: She asked where was the dam.
She asked where the dam was.
She asked where the dam was?
She asked, where the dam was.
practice.explain: Statement word order and a full stop.

practice.q: Report this: “I am tired,” said Ali.
options: Ali said that I am tired.
Ali said that he was tired.
practice.explain: ‘I’ becomes ‘he’ and ‘am’ becomes ‘was’.

practice.q: Which word can report a yes/no question?
practice.explain: ‘If’ or ‘whether’ report yes/no questions.

practice.q: What punctuation ends an indirect question?
practice.explain: An indirect question is a statement, so it ends with a full stop.

grammar.title: Word classes
grammar.intro: Every word in a sentence has a job, like players in a team. When you know each word’s job, you can build sentences that are clear, correct and powerful.
points: **Nouns** name things (energy, panels). **Pronouns** replace nouns (they, it).
**Verbs** show actions or states (generate, is). **Adjectives** describe nouns (clean, solar).
**Adverbs** describe verbs, adjectives or other adverbs (cleanly, very).
**Prepositions** show position or time (in, on, of). **Conjunctions** join words or clauses (and, but, because).
**Determiners** come before nouns to show which or how many (the, a, some, this, its).

examples.text: **The** (determiner) **wind** (noun) **turns** (verb) **huge** (adjective) **blades** (noun) **quickly** (adverb).
examples.note: Each word has its own job.

examples.text: They built **a** farm **on** the hill **and** it worked.
examples.note: A determiner, a preposition and a conjunction.

examples.text: We **paint** walls. / We bought some **paint**.
examples.note: The same word can be a verb or a noun, depending on its job.

grammar.tip: Do not guess from the word alone. Look at how it is used in the sentence.

practice.q: What word class is ‘solar’ in ‘solar panels’?
practice.explain: ‘Solar’ describes the panels, so it is an adjective.

practice.q: Which word is a preposition? ‘The panels sit on the roof.’
practice.explain: ‘On’ shows position.

practice.q: Which word is a determiner? ‘Some farms use biogas.’
practice.explain: ‘Some’ comes before the noun and tells us how many.

practice.q: What word class is ‘they’ in ‘They built a dam’?
practice.explain: ‘They’ replaces a noun, so it is a pronoun.

practice.q: Which word is a conjunction? ‘It is cheap and it is clean.’
practice.explain: ‘And’ joins the two clauses.

grammar.title: Verb forms
grammar.intro: Verbs are shape-shifters! The same verb can take several forms, and each one helps you to show exactly when and how something happens.
points: The **base form**: generate, spin, capture.
The **third person singular present**: generates, spins, captures.
The **present participle** (-ing form): generating, spinning, capturing. It is used with ‘is’, ‘are’ or ‘was’.
The **simple past**: generated, spun, captured.
The **past participle**: generated, spun, captured. It is used with ‘has’, ‘have’ or ‘had’, and in the passive.

examples.text: The turbine **spins**.
examples.note: Third person singular present.

examples.text: The turbines **are spinning**.
examples.note: Present participle with ‘are’.

examples.text: The panels **have captured** sunlight all day.
examples.note: Past participle with ‘have’.

grammar.tip: Irregular verbs change in surprising ways: write, wrote, written. Learn them in sets of three.

practice.q: Which is the present participle of ‘generate’?
practice.explain: The present participle ends in -ing.

practice.q: Choose the correct form: ‘Solar power ___ more popular every year.’

practice.explain: After ‘have’, use the past participle: built.

units.title: Classic Words
units.overview: Some stories are so good that people keep reading them for more than a hundred years. In this unit you will step into two classic novels: Mark Twain’s tale of Tom Sawyer and a very clever trick with a fence, and Frances Hodgson Burnett’s The Secret Garden, where a lonely girl discovers a hidden, forgotten garden. You will explore how writers engage readers, compare written and spoken English, use the perfect tenses, and write a character description and a story of your own.
objectives: Identify techniques writers use to engage readers, such as vivid description, dialogue and a strong narrative voice.
Explain the differences between written and spoken English, and change dialogue into reported speech.
Understand and use idioms.
Spell words with the /j/ sound written j, g and dge.
Identify the voice of the narrator and the writer in a story.
Use the present perfect, past perfect and future perfect tenses.
Choose powerful words, perform a character, and write a character description and a story.

texts.title: The Glorious Whitewasher (from The Adventures of Tom Sawyer)
texts.kind: Classic novel extract by Mark Twain
texts.summary: On a bright Saturday morning, Tom Sawyer has to whitewash Aunt Polly’s long fence instead of playing. When his friend Ben comes along, ready to tease him, Tom pretends that painting is a rare privilege that only a gifted boy could do. Soon Ben is begging for a turn and paying for it, and by the end of the day Tom is sitting in the shade while his friends do the work.

texts.title: The Secret Garden
texts.kind: Classic novel extract by Frances Hodgson Burnett
texts.summary: Mary Lennox, a lonely and cross girl who once lived in India, now lives at Misselthwaite Manor in Yorkshire. She finds her way into a hidden garden that nobody has looked after for years. Its roses seem dead, but Mary discovers that some plants are still alive, and caring for the garden begins to change her. Martha, a cheerful maid, speaks in a Yorkshire dialect.

vocab.example: The Secret Garden is a classic.

vocab.meaning: To paint something with a white mixture, often on walls or fences.
vocab.example: Tom had to whitewash the fence.

vocab.meaning: A deep, quiet sadness.
vocab.example: A deep melancholy settled over Tom.

vocab.meaning: Not wanting to do something.
vocab.example: Tom handed over the brush with pretend reluctance.

vocab.meaning: A phrase whose meaning is different from the meanings of its separate words.
vocab.example: ‘Call it a day’ means stop working for now.

vocab.meaning: A form of a language spoken in a particular area, with its own words and grammar.
vocab.example: Martha speaks in a Yorkshire dialect.

vocab.meaning: The voice that tells the story.
vocab.example: The narrator describes Mary’s feelings.

vocab.meaning: Not cared for over a long time.
vocab.example: The neglected garden was full of tangled roses.

vocab.meaning: A verb form made with has, have, had or will have and a past participle.
vocab.example: ‘She had found the key’ is in the past perfect tense.

vocab.meaning: To catch and hold someone’s interest.
vocab.example: A strong opening line engages the reader.

grammar.title: Differences between written and spoken English
grammar.intro: We do not write the way we talk, and we do not talk the way we write! Clever writers use spoken English in dialogue to bring characters to life, and standard written English everywhere else.
points: **Spoken English** often uses **contractions** (ain’t, don’t), **informal words**, **fillers** (well, you know) and **incomplete sentences**.
**Written English** is usually more **formal**, with complete sentences and standard grammar.
Writers use spoken English in **dialogue** to show a character’s personality, background and **dialect**.
When you change dialogue into **reported speech**, use standard written English.

examples.text: “Hello, old chap, you got to work, hey?”

examples.note: Written: formal reported speech.

grammar.tip: Spoken English is not wrong. It just belongs in dialogue, not in formal writing.

grammar.title: Perfect tenses
grammar.intro: The perfect tenses are like bridges in time. They link one moment to another. Once you master them, you can show your reader exactly how events connect.
points: The **present perfect** (has/have + past participle) links the past to now: ‘I **have read** this book.’
The **past perfect** (had + past participle) shows an action that happened **before** another past action: ‘The roses **had spread** before Mary arrived.’
The **future perfect** (will have + past participle) shows that something will be finished by a time in the future: ‘By spring, we **will have planted** seeds.’
Learn irregular past participles: seen, flown, grown, written, done.

examples.text: Mary **has found** a secret garden.
examples.note: Present perfect: the finding is linked to now.

examples.text: Nobody **had opened** the door for ten years.
examples.note: Past perfect: before Mary came.

grammar.tip: Look for has/have, had or will have. Then check that the verb after it is a past participle.

Then you will meet two young people who describe their everyday lives in Thailand and Russia. You will learn the features of autobiographies, how to use verb tenses and shift between them correctly, and you will write an autobiographical essay about yourself.

grammar.title: Verb tenses
grammar.intro: Tenses are the clock inside every sentence. When you write about your life, you will travel between the past, the present and the future, so let’s make sure you always know what time it is!
points: The **simple past** describes finished actions: ‘She **walked** to the pump.’
The **past continuous** describes an action in progress in the past: ‘I **was drawing** water.’
The **simple present** describes habits and facts: ‘Children **learn** words quickly.’
The **past perfect** describes an action before another past action: ‘I **had learnt** a few words.’
The **future** can be shown with **will** or **going to**: ‘I **will be** an engineer.’

examples.text: My teacher **arrived** in March.
examples.note: Simple past: a finished event.

examples.text: I **was stringing** beads when she came in.
examples.note: Past continuous: an action in progress.

examples.text: I **live** in Bangkok and I **play** tennis.
examples.note: Simple present: facts and habits.

grammar.tip: Autobiographies mostly use the past tense, but present facts about your life now are in the present tense.

practice.explain: was + -ing form = past continuous.

practice.explain: It states a general fact, so it is in the simple present.

grammar.title: Verb tense shifts
grammar.intro: Imagine a story that keeps jumping between yesterday and today for no reason. Confusing! Good writers only change tense when the time really changes, and you are about to become one of them.
points: Keep to **one main tense** in a paragraph unless the time of the action changes.
An **unnecessary tense shift** is a mistake: ‘I **went** home and **eat** dinner.’ ✗
A **correct tense shift** has a reason: ‘My name **means** “little bee” because my father **was** a beekeeper.’
Facts that are still true use the **present tense**, even in a past-tense paragraph.

examples.text: I returned the book and the librarian **was** happy.
examples.note: Both verbs stay in the past.

examples.text: My parents named me Xoli, which **means** ‘one who forgives’.
examples.note: Correct shift: the meaning is still true today.

examples.text: Yesterday I did my homework and then I **went** out.
examples.note: ‘Yesterday’ keeps both actions in the past.

grammar.tip: Read your paragraph and underline each verb. Is every change of tense for a good reason?

units.title: All the World’s a Stage
units.overview: Lights up, curtain up! In our final unit you will read two play scripts. The first is an adapted scene from Shakespeare’s King Lear, in which an ageing king asks his daughters to say how much they love him, with dramatic results. The second is a modern play about a brave young climber called Yusuf. You will learn the features of play scripts, use active and passive verb forms, explore Shakespeare’s famous phrases, and finally write a play script of your own.
objectives: Identify the features of play scripts, including the cast list, stage directions, acts, scenes, asides and monologues.

texts.title: King Lear (adapted)

Goneril and Regan flatter him with grand speeches, but his youngest daughter, Cordelia, refuses to exaggerate and simply tells the truth. Furious, Lear gives her nothing, and when the loyal Earl of Kent speaks up for her, Lear banishes him too. The scene explores truth and flattery, and wise and unwise decisions.

Yusuf has not told his mother, who does not want him to climb. On the mountain, the boys find an injured man and must decide how to help him, and Yusuf has to face his fears.

Write your play script with a cast list, stage directions and dialogue.
Revise and edit, then perform it with your group.
wb.tip: Read your script aloud to check that the dialogue sounds natural.

cards.front: What does King Lear ask his daughters to do?
cards.back: To say how much they love him, so that he can divide his kingdom among them.

cards.front: Why is Cordelia given nothing?
cards.back: She refuses to flatter her father and simply tells the truth, which makes Lear furious.

cards.front: What happens to the Earl of Kent?
cards.back: He speaks up for Cordelia, and Lear banishes him.

cards.front: What is an aside?
cards.back: Words a character says to the audience that the other characters on stage cannot hear.

cards.front: Why is Yusuf’s climb on Jabal Sawda so important to him?
cards.back: His father died in a climbing accident there, and Yusuf has to face his fears and his feelings about it.

cards.front: Which prefix goes before roots starting with l, m or p, and r?
cards.back: il- before l (illegal), im- before m or p (immortal, impossible), ir- before r (irregular).

cards.front: What is the difference between hyperbole and a euphemism?
cards.back: Hyperbole exaggerates. A euphemism says something unpleasant in a gentle way.

practice.q: What are stage directions?
options: Instructions for how actors move and speak
practice.explain: Stage directions tell actors what to do and how to do it.

practice.q: Which sentence is passive?
practice.explain: ‘was banished’ is a form of ‘be’ plus a past participle.

practice.q: Which daughter refuses to flatter King Lear?
practice.explain: Cordelia tells the truth instead of flattering him.

practice.q: Which word means ‘not legal’?
practice.explain: We use il- before words that start with l.

practice.q: What does ‘a wild goose chase’ mean?
options: A hopeless search for something you will not find
practice.explain: It means a long, useless search.

practice.q: Which is a euphemism?
options: I’m so hungry I could eat a horse.
practice.explain: ‘Passed away’ is a gentle way of saying ‘died’.

practice.q: Why does Yusuf feel bad at the start of the climb?
options: He has not told his mother about the climb
practice.explain: Yusuf feels bad about not telling his mother.

practice.q: What is an aside?
options: A long speech to other characters
Words spoken to the audience that other characters cannot hear
practice.explain: An aside shares a character’s private thoughts with the audience.

grammar.title: Active and passive verb forms
grammar.intro: You met the passive voice back in Unit 2. Now let’s take it further. Playwrights and writers switch between active and passive to decide what the audience should notice first. You can do the same!
points: In the **active voice**, the subject does the action: ‘Lear **banished** Kent.’
In the **passive voice**, the subject receives the action: ‘Kent **was banished** by Lear.’
Form the passive with **be** in the right tense + the **past participle**: is made, was made, will be made.
The passive puts the **focus** on the person or thing affected, or hides who did the action.

examples.text: The courtiers **entertained** the king. → The king **was entertained** by the courtiers.
examples.note: The focus moves to the king.

examples.text: The seamstresses **make** the robes. → The robes **are made** by the seamstresses.
examples.note: Present tense in both.

examples.text: The rope **is pulled** firmly to test the knot.
examples.note: The focus is on the rope; we do not need to say who pulled it.

grammar.tip: When you change a sentence, keep the tense the same: ‘will banish’ becomes ‘will be banished’.

practice.q: Change to the passive: ‘Lear will banish Kent.’
options: Kent will be banished by Lear.
practice.explain: Future passive: will be + past participle.

practice.q: Change to the active: ‘The play was watched by many people.’
practice.explain: The doers, ‘many people’, become the subject.

practice.q: Which sentence is active?
options: The crown is worn by Lear.
practice.explain: Kent is the subject and does the action.

practice.q: Which is the correct passive form? ‘The robes ___ by the seamstresses last year.’
practice.explain: ‘Last year’ needs the past: were made.

practice.q: Why might a writer use the passive?
options: To focus on the person or thing affected by the action
practice.explain: The passive moves the focus to the receiver of the action.

grammar.title: Prefixes that create antonyms
grammar.intro: Here is a quick way to double your vocabulary: add a prefix and you have an opposite! Learn a few simple rules and you will choose the right prefix every time.
points: **un-**, **dis-** and **mis-** create opposites: unhappy, dishonest, misunderstand.
**il-** is used before words beginning with **l**: illegal, illogical.
**im-** is used before words beginning with **m** or **p**: immortal, impossible.
**ir-** is used before words beginning with **r**: irregular, irrelevant.
**mis-** often means ‘wrongly’ or ‘badly’: misbehave, misprint.

examples.text: Lear thought Cordelia was **un**grateful.
examples.note: un- + grateful.

examples.text: Climbing alone at night would be **ir**responsible.
examples.note: ir- before r.

examples.text: Kent **dis**obeyed the king’s order to stay silent.
examples.note: dis- + obey.

grammar.tip: Keep both letters when a prefix meets the same letter: il + legal = illegal, mis + spell = misspell.

practice.q: Which is the antonym of ‘possible’?
practice.explain: We use im- before p.

practice.q: Which is the antonym of ‘regular’?
practice.explain: We use ir- before r.

practice.q: Which is the antonym of ‘logical’?
practice.explain: We use il- before l.

practice.q: What does ‘misquote’ mean?
practice.explain: mis- means wrongly.

practice.q: Which word is spelt correctly?
practice.explain: mis + spell = misspell. Keep the s from mis- and the s from spell.
